pages.x: Porfirio Díaz had ruled Mexico for over 30 years. He brought in railways and foreign money, but most of the land belonged to a few great estates, worked by millions of farmers trapped in debt and poverty. In 1910, at 80, he had himself re-elected yet again, after jailing his rival.

The rival, Francisco Madero, a rich landowner's son who believed in fair elections, escaped to Texas and called for a rising on 20 November 1910. Rebels rose across the country, and in May 1911 Díaz sailed into exile. Madero was elected president, but in 1913 his own general, Victoriano Huerta, overthrew him and had him shot.

In the south Emiliano Zapata, a horse trainer from Morelos, led farmers to take back the land that sugar estates had taken from their villages. His Plan of Ayala demanded that the land go to those who worked it. His cry was land and liberty, and he fought every government that would not give it.

In the north Pancho Villa, a former bandit, led the Division of the North with cavalry, trains and even a deal with an American film company to film his battles. In 1914 the armies of Villa and Zapata drove out Huerta and met in Mexico City, where they posed for photographs in the president's palace.

Then the winners fought each other. Battles, executions, hunger and in the end the flu killed perhaps a million Mexicans, and hundreds of thousands more fled north. Women soldiers, the soldaderas, cooked, nursed and fought beside the men.
pages.of: Mexicans died, of war, hunger and disease

pages.x: When the United States backed his rival, Villa raided the town of Columbus, New Mexico, in March 1916, killing 18 Americans. General John Pershing chased him through northern Mexico for almost a year with thousands of soldiers, aeroplanes and trucks, and never caught him.

In 1917 the winning side, led by Venustiano Carranza, wrote a new constitution at Querétaro. It promised land reform, free schooling, an eight-hour working day and the right to strike, and it put the nation's oil and minerals in its own hands. It is still Mexico's constitution today.

Peace came hard. Zapata was lured into a trap and shot in 1919, Carranza was killed in 1920, and Villa was gunned down in his car in 1923. Only in the 1930s, under President Lázaro Cárdenas, was most of the land finally shared out.

The revolution shaped modern Mexico: its constitution, its land reform, its pride in its Native and mixed roots, painted in the great murals of Diego Rivera, and the party that grew out of it, which ruled for 71 years. Zapata is still a hero to farmers and rebels across Latin America.
pts: Zapata fought for land and liberty
